title: Chick Webb's encouragement: "be yourself"
summary: Jones says Webb's advice to keep his naturalness and develop his own style kept him from leaving, and he taught him discipline.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Hey, by the way, Jo, I just want to make a note. Don't feel that you have to sit here. Walk around and do anything you want to do just as long as you say what you want to say.
No, I'm cool here with my water here.
I want you to walk around, do anything that you want to, so that you can express yourself the way you do. This is for the records here.
Of course. But Milt, this man saw what I was trying to do in the Basie band. He saw the material I had to work with. He would have loved to have had the

material that I had to work with. But without this man's encouragement, without this man telling me what I was supposed to do, you wouldn't have seen me sitting here today. I was ready to leave and go back. I would probably have took up some scholastic career, gone back to Omaha. I didn't care. But he encouraged me and he told me of things to come. There are a lot of things that he told me what to do and told me what I must do, that I have never forgotten. He said, "It isn't a form of humility, it's just a form of don't lose your naturalness. Be yourself." I said, "Thank you. That's what my grandmother always told me, to be myself." He said, "You don't have to do this because somebody's doing something like that. You just go on and you develop what you develop, and pretty soon you'll have a style of Jo Jones, because you have a wealth, and I'm looking at that." He showed it to me. These are the kind of conversations I had with Mr. Webb; when everybody else was going to the after hours spots I would be with Mr. Webb. He would be talking, but I would be listening. He showed me and he'd come out and check me out and see what I was doing. Because I remember we was in Boston once and he came down, he'd stand around with his little wraparound coat on. The last time that he came around we was in Detroit and he came around to the Graystone Ballroom and he was falling through town. He heard the band and we went to the Norwood Hotel and we went across to the street

to get the sausages and grits and what have you. He turned around and asked me, "Give me a cigarette." I said, "Wait a minute. Ain't you got enough money to get those cigarettes?" He said, "I won't buy no cigarettes." And he taught me all that too. He said, "Don't buy no cigarettes." I said, "Yes, but you're the great bandleader." But this man taught me something that I had almost forgotten - he taught me discipline. He taught me the character. He told me how important the drum was.
